Ok so I'm getting PISSED OFF about the "first-principles thinking" discourse that Thiel started making  popular (less recently) and then Elon (more recently) and which people quacking about IRONICALLY have no idea what they're on about, so here's how it actually works:
↓
1384410913479004161 [2021-04-20] @nosilverv 💜 25
To get how it works we must get what ISN'T first-principles thinking so that we can DISTINGUISH IT from first-principles thinking. And for THAT we have to figure out a particular ASPECT of thinking that we get from SEMIOTICS (the study of hows signs and symbols create meaning)
↓
1384410915085373441 [2021-04-20] @nosilverv 💜 10
I know this seems ANNOYING but it will pay off I promise
↓
1384410918491201536 [2021-04-20] @nosilverv 💜 19 🔁 4
So, semiotics, or, specifically, the semiotic triangle below. It distinguishes between THREE THINGS:
Signifiers or signs
Referents
Meaning https://t.co/ZLBa8a3wtl
Images:
  - [Image #0] The image shows a diagram known as the semiotic triangle, illustrating the relationships between three key concepts in semiotics. To reproduce this diagram, draw a triangle with three vertices labeled: 
    1. "Signifier/Physical Sign/Representamen (e.g., word, gesture, object, picture)" at the top, 
    2. "Signified/Referent/Object (e.g., object, event, idea, concept)" at the bottom left, and 
    3. "Signification/Meaning/Interpretant (e.g., mental interpretation of that meaning)" at the bottom right. 
    
    Connect the top vertex to the two bottom vertices with lines, and draw a line between the two bottom vertices, making it slightly thicker than the other two lines.
↓
1384410925113937921 [2021-04-20] @nosilverv 💜 29 🔁 3
I think this is one of those things that's easier to learn via demonstration so here's a bunch of examples: https://t.co/YW4bE4Txg1
Images:
  - [Image #0] The image is a slide that illustrates the concept of semiotics, featuring three distinct sections. 
    
    The title "The Concept....." is displayed in yellow text at the top left. Below it, three images are arranged horizontally: a photograph of a red rose, a graphic of two red roses, and a red heart with the text "I Love" above it. Each image is accompanied by a label and description in yellow text below.
    
    The first image, labeled "REFERENT," is described as "The actual thing referred to." The second image, labeled "SIGNIFIER," is described as "The physical form of the sign (word or image)." The third image, labeled "SIGNIFIED," is described as "The mental image that enters our mind when you see the signifier."
    
    The background of the slide is black, providing a clear contrast to the yellow text and colorful images.
  - [Image #1] The image is a diagram illustrating the relationship between a symbol, its referent, and the thought or reference associated with it.
    
    The diagram consists of three main components: "SYMBOL," "REFERENT," and "THOUGHT OR REFERENCE." The "SYMBOL" is represented by a silhouette of a tree, labeled as the "Signifier." The "REFERENT" is depicted as a realistic image of a tree, referred to as the "Object." The "THOUGHT OR REFERENCE" is symbolized by a head with a gear inside, signifying the "Signified." 
    
    Arrows connect these elements, indicating their relationships. The arrow between "SYMBOL" and "THOUGHT OR REFERENCE" is labeled "Symbolises," while the arrow between "THOUGHT OR REFERENCE" and "REFERENT" is labeled "Refers to." Another arrow connects "SYMBOL" and "REFERENT," forming a circular flow. The background of the diagram is white, providing a clean and simple visual representation of the concept.
  - [Image #2] The image presents a humorous take on the concept of semiotics, a field of study that examines how meaning is created and communicated through language and symbols. The title "So true 🤷‍♀️👀" is accompanied by a graphic of a hand with its palm facing outward, followed by the subtitle "When bae tells you something." 
    
    The image is divided into three sections, each representing a different aspect of communication:
    
    *   **What she says**: This section is labeled "Signifier" and includes three bullet points that describe the signifier as:
        *   The 'shape' of word
        *   The sound-image
        *   Phonic component of word
    *   **What you think she means**: This section is labeled "Signified" and includes two bullet points that describe the signified as:
        *   Concept or meaning invoked by the word
        *   Ideational component of word
    *   **What she really means**: This section is labeled "Referent" and includes two bullet points that describe the referent as:
        *   Actual real-life object that is referred to
        *   Transcends 'concept' as physically present item
    
    The image uses a lighthearted tone to illustrate the complexities of communication, highlighting the potential disconnect between what is said, what is meant, and what is understood. The use of the term "bae" (a colloquialism for "before anyone else") adds a playful touch to the image, making it more relatable and engaging. Overall, the image provides a humorous and accessible introduction to the concepts of semiotics and the challenges of effective communication.

1384410927001374722 [2021-04-20] @nosilverv 💜 15
The basic distinction is <word>, <things the word refer to in the world>, <image that the word pops in your head>.

Denotation and connotation point at the same thing:
↓
1384410928976904193 [2021-04-20] @nosilverv 💜 13 [(SEED) type=semantic_search]
Think of the word "Trump". It's nothing but a SIGN that POINTS at that particular human individual. But the signified, the meaning that comes to your head, is so much more than that.
↓
1384410930642100224 [2021-04-20] @nosilverv 💜 23 🔁 1
And this is the crucial point and if you get this you get it all, the idea is that there is a difference between what the word/sign STRICTLY refers to and to the IMAGE that appears in your head.
↓
1384410932286214145 [2021-04-20] @nosilverv 💜 21 🔁 2
And, AND, AND - People think they're dealing with the former when they're dealing with the latter. That is, you get a word, something that MEANS something else and you think you correctly dereference it when you don't.
↓
1384410933942947840 [2021-04-20] @nosilverv 💜 34 🔁 1
The word POINTS at something in the world. If you dereference to a particular meaning in your head, to a caricature that is already there, that you usually got from society, you're not doing first-principles thinking.
↓
1384410935578828803 [2021-04-20] @nosilverv 💜 10
If, on the other hand, you dereference to the actual extension of the concept then you are. Here's an example to make it simpler:
↓
1384410939135508485 [2021-04-20] @nosilverv 💜 21 🔁 1
Here Musk's talking about the cost of batteries and how he got it down and why other's couldn't. Why? They were modelling batteries 'from the outside' as it were. https://t.co/01niAtXQ40
Images:
  - [Image #0] The image contains a text passage that explains Elon Musk's approach to understanding the cost of batteries. The text is transcribed as follows:
    
    "Musk used the cost of batteries as an example. 'People would say, 'Historically it's cost $600 per kilowatt-hour, and so it's not going to be much better than that in the future.' And you say, 'No, what are the batteries made of?' First principles means you say, 'Okay, what are the material constituents of the batteries?'"
    
    This text passage describes Musk's method of analyzing the cost of batteries by breaking down their material components, rather than relying on historical trends.
↓
1384410941241057280 [2021-04-20] @nosilverv 💜 11 🔁 1
More precisely: when you read the word "batteries" I'm sure you had a particular image coming to mind. When you read that word it DEREFERENCES to that signified, or meaning.
↓
1384410942876889088 [2021-04-20] @nosilverv 💜 13 🔁 1
HOWEVER, HOWEVER a battery is, no more and no less than a device consisting of one or more electrochemical cells with external connections that powers electrical devices.
↓
1384410944462336002 [2021-04-20] @nosilverv 💜 16
Do you see how that definition, that dereferencing, CONTAINS your specific image but also SO MUCH MORE BEYOND IT? That's the key:
↓
1384410946005786624 [2021-04-20] @nosilverv 💜 23 🔁 1
your specific image was gotten from somewhere and made by someone for some reason. It might be the one that you need, it might not. But the more extensive dereferencing gives you way more OPTIONS. Using it Musk could make a NEW battery that was much cheaper.
↓
1384410947608064002 [2021-04-20] @nosilverv 💜 60 🔁 10
And herein the benefit of first-principles thinking: if you move BEYOND your images, your caricatures, and go 'down a level of abstraction' to the actual mechanism of how a thing works or why it is what it is then the space of possibilities is MUCH larger.

I attended Hereticon in 2022, and I had an experience there that made a truly deep impact on me. Getting to the conclusion was a trek for me, so you’re going to have to listen to the whole story.

===

1657613626826702848 [2023-05-14] @eshear 💜 278 🔁 19
Interregnum: I encourage you to actually consider this question. What is it that grounds out truth for you? This isn’t a trick question, go with the obvious and naive answer.
↓
1657613628282138626 [2023-05-14] @eshear 💜 177 🔁 4
Srsly think about your answer (and what other people might answer) before you keep reading. It’s more fun that way and you learn more.
↓
1657613629548826627 [2023-05-14] @eshear 💜 343 🔁 29
So eventually he comes to his answer. When someone presents an idea, he connects with them. He looks in their eyes. He considers their motivations. And if their argument is internally consistent with itself. And if all the signs are green, he trusts them and that’s truth.
↓
1657613630974877696 [2023-05-14] @eshear 💜 486 🔁 23
This just blew me away. It’s a fundamentally social theory of truth. Truth is based on credible arguments presented by trustworthy people. 

That is not what truth is to me, at all.
↓
1657613632296095745 [2023-05-14] @eshear 💜 291 🔁 12
For me, the gold standard of truth is what I can see, hear, taste, smell, feel for myself. What is “true” is what my current conceptual model of the world can infer from that data.
↓
1657613633902481408 [2023-05-14] @eshear 💜 239 🔁 8
(Actually truth is whatever reflects the underlying nature of reality, we are talking here only about our current best guess at truth, but this is an unavoidable distinction for finite beings who cannot know Truth)
↓
1657613635324379138 [2023-05-14] @eshear 💜 335 🔁 8
I’d never heard someone actually say the quiet part out loud like that before. I think perhaps many people have his relationship to the truth, but with more normal choices for people to trust, and therefore more standard beliefs (and more correct ones IMO).
↓
1657613636599443456 [2023-05-14] @eshear 💜 215 🔁 4
At this point I completely lost interest in discussing space and viruses and etc w him any further. Because I’d understood what had been driving me to ask and ask…I’d figured out how this seemingly smart man had come to conclusions that seemed so insane.
↓
1657613637887094785 [2023-05-14] @eshear 💜 396 🔁 39
I’ve come up with names for these two sides (tho I’d be interested in better ones, if anyone has them): team words-mean-things, and team alliances.
↓
1657613639195705344 [2023-05-14] @eshear 💜 282 🔁 12
The sense-data theory of truth leads to team words-mean-things. Because the goal of words, at least outside of art, is to convey sense data impressions and models inferred from them. And to do this well, one must care fanatically that your use of the word is the same as theirs.
↓
1657613640437223424 [2023-05-14] @eshear 💜 235 🔁 10 [(SEED) type=semantic_search]
The canonical sign you are talking to a words-mean-things person is the exasperated sigh followed by “wait but i thought you said X was Y, but now it’s not Y?”
↓
1657613641980710912 [2023-05-14] @eshear 💜 217 🔁 9
The credible-talk-from-trusted-sources theory of truth by contrast leads to team alliances. Because if you get the words a little wrong, it’s fine, you can trust the ultimate conclusions regardless as long as you can trust them. As long as they’re on your team.
↓
1657613643297746945 [2023-05-14] @eshear 💜 294 🔁 8
The canonical sign you’re talking to a team alliances person is when they seem more interested in figuring out whether you’re on their team than whether the details of your words make sense. “Is he a good guy?”
↓
1657613644669280256 [2023-05-14] @eshear 💜 282 🔁 8
Alliances : Words-Mean-Things :: Mimesis : First Principles

Given my team, my take feels anti-alliances. But learning-via-trust has a lot to recommend it. I don’t think one is “better”. But know yourself, know who you’re talking to, and connect at their level.
↓
